narrative:
Your loan application was denied because our model predicts a 51% chance that you represent a bad credit risk, meaning it sees a slight tilt toward potential repayment issues based on your overall financial profile. This decision hinges heavily on the status of your checking account, which shows as "<0 DM"—a situation shared by only about 20% of approved applicants, most of whom have no account issues or small positive balances. In contrast, your requested loan duration of 12 months is shorter than the 19-month average for those approved, your credit amount of 1108 DM is well below their typical 2887 DM, and your installment rate of 4% edges above their 2.9% average, but these factors alone didn't tip the scales against you.

To understand why, imagine "what if" scenarios where we tweak just a few details about your situation—these are called counterfactuals, and they reveal the minimal changes needed to flip the model's prediction to "good credit" and approve your loan. We generated one such scenario, and it pinpointed a single key change: improving your checking account status from its current negative balance to having no account problems at all. Notably, this feature changed in 100% of the counterfactuals, while 16 others—like your credit history of no credits or all paid, repair-purpose loan, savings under 100 DM, 4-7 years of employment, real estate property, own housing, two existing credits, skilled job, no telephone, and others—stayed exactly the same and never needed adjustment.

This tells us your checking account status is by far the most important factor driving the rejection; it's the linchpin that, when fixed, overrides everything else in your profile, which otherwise aligns reasonably with approved applicants—for instance, your real estate ownership matches 31% of them, your skilled job fits 65%, and no other installment plans or debtors is typical. Compared to those approved, you're also close on residence duration and dependents, but that account issue stands out as the outlier pulling you down.

The good news is this points to a straightforward, realistic fix: resolve any overdraft or issues with your checking account to reach a "no problems" status, something achievable by paying down negatives or building a small positive balance, as 50% of approved applicants have no account issues and 23% hold 0-200 DM. No need to alter your loan amount, extend the duration, switch jobs, or add guarantors—the model would approve you as-is once that one feature shifts. With this change, your profile would mirror successful applicants even more closely, boosting your predicted good credit odds above the threshold. Reapplying after addressing your checking account could very well turn things around for you.
